jurisdiction.name: Group of Seven
jurisdiction.overview: Informal forum of seven economies and the EU, with a rotating presidency and no secretariat. Its AI texts are political commitments by Leaders and Ministers.

narrative.summary: The G7's AI texts come from the Hiroshima AI Process launched under Japan's 2023 presidency. On 30 October 2023 Leaders welcomed the International Guiding Principles and the International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems; on 1 and 6 December 2023 Ministers and Leaders endorsed the Comprehensive Policy Framework, which extends the principles to all AI actors. All are voluntary, and the Code is addressed to organisations rather than governments. A wider Hiroshima AI Process Friends Group of countries supports the process; it is not counted as adoption here.
narrative.review_notes: The Hiroshima AI Process site of Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, which publishes the full texts, was searched, and membership is taken from Global Affairs Canada's G7 page; Japan's foreign ministry site was unavailable. The Friends Group list (69 countries and the EU as of August 2026) is kept as context, since members support 'the spirit' of the process rather than adopting the texts, and later outputs (the March 2024 ministerial declaration and the reporting framework) are pending.

instruments.official_title: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems
instruments.english_title: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems
instruments.publisher_name: Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, Japan (2023 G7 presidency)
instruments.current_status: Published in full on the Hiroshima AI Process site of Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, the ministry that led the process for the 2023 Japanese G7 presidency (the G7 has no secretariat). Welcomed by G7 Leaders in the G7 Leaders' Statement on the Hiroshima AI Process of 30 October 2023, to which it is attached; the document itself carries no date, so the date of that statement is used. Leaders 'call on organizations developing advanced AI systems to commit to the application of the International Code of Conduct'. Voluntary for organisations; a political commitment, not legally binding.
instruments.scope: G7 members; organisations developing or using advanced AI systems
instruments.summary: Voluntary code of 11 actions for organisations developing the most advanced AI systems, including foundation models and generative AI: risk identification and mitigation across the lifecycle, post-deployment vulnerability and misuse monitoring, public transparency reporting, incident information sharing, risk-based governance policies, security controls, content authentication/provenance, research on safety, and data and IP protections. G7 Leaders called on organisations to commit to it; it builds on the OECD AI Principles and is to be reviewed as a living document.

instruments.current_status: Published in full on the Hiroshima AI Process site of Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, the ministry that led the process for the 2023 Japanese G7 presidency (the G7 has no secretariat). Welcomed by G7 Leaders in the G7 Leaders' Statement on the Hiroshima AI Process of 30 October 2023, to which it is attached; the document itself carries no date, so the date of that statement is used. Leaders 'call on organizations developing advanced AI systems to commit to the application of the International Code of Conduct'. Voluntary for organisations; a political commitment, not legally binding.
instruments.scope: G7 members; organisations developing or using advanced AI systems
instruments.summary: Eleven non-exhaustive guiding principles for organisations developing and using advanced AI systems (foundation models, generative AI), from academia, civil society, private and public sectors, building on the OECD AI Principles. Covers lifecycle risk management, misuse monitoring, transparency on capabilities and limitations, incident sharing, governance policies, security, content provenance, safety research, priority on global challenges, technical standards and data protection. States that jurisdictions may implement it in their own ways.

instruments.official_title: Hiroshima AI Process Comprehensive Policy Framework
instruments.english_title: Hiroshima AI Process Comprehensive Policy Framework
instruments.issuing_authority: G7 Digital and Tech Ministers; endorsed by G7 Leaders
instruments.publisher_name: Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, Japan (2023 G7 presidency)
instruments.current_status: Published in full on the Hiroshima AI Process site of Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, the ministry that led the process for the 2023 Japanese G7 presidency (the G7 has no secretariat). Endorsed by the G7 Digital and Tech Ministers in their statement of 1 December 2023 ('We endorse the attached Hiroshima AI Process Comprehensive Policy Framework') and by G7 Leaders in their statement of 6 December 2023. Annex 1 extends the Guiding Principles to all AI actors. A political commitment; not legally binding.
instruments.scope: G7 members; organisations developing or using advanced AI systems
instruments.summary: Framework of four elements: the OECD report towards a G7 common understanding on generative AI, the International Guiding Principles (extended to all AI actors in Annex 1), the International Code of Conduct for organisations developing advanced AI, and project-based cooperation on AI. Ministers encourage all AI actors to follow the Guiding Principles as appropriate and call on developers of advanced AI to commit to the Code of Conduct.
